analysis.one_liner: Phases out the federal estate tax over ten years, ending the tax on very large inheritances.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 274-154 with 58 Democrats joining, but the Senate never voted; an estate-tax phase-out was instead enacted inside the 2001 tax cut law.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes outright, effective 2011, while cutting estate tax rates each year in the meantime and raising the amount an estate can pass tax-free to $1 million by 2006. It also replaces the current rule that resets the value of inherited property at death with a 'carryover basis' rule, and adds reporting duties for large transfers. The House passed it with broad support, but the Senate never took a vote; the estate-tax phase-out instead became part of the broader 2001 tax cut law (H.R. 1836, cross-referenced in the House action history).
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to estates large enough to owe the tax. Under the bill's own schedule the tax would only apply above a $1 million exemption by 2006, so the gains concentrate on multi-million-dollar estates, including the very largest, which see rates fall from 55% toward repeal. Family farms and closely held businesses are the bill's stated beneficiaries and do get targeted relief, such as longer to pay estate tax.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes entirely, effective for deaths after December 31, 2010, after a decade of phased rate cuts.

Before repeal, the bill cuts the top estate tax rate to 50% starting in 2002, then reduces rates further each year through 2010, and replaces the old unified credit with an exemption reaching $1,000,000 by 2006.

Family-owned businesses get targeted relief: closely held businesses with up to 45 partners or shareholders (up from 15) qualify for extended estate-tax payment, and the conservation-easement estate tax rule is expanded to cover land farther from cities and parks.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government loses the revenue it currently collects from the largest estates, which has to be made up by other taxpayers or through less federal spending. Heirs also take on new recordkeeping, because the bill replaces the step-up in basis with carryover basis and requires information returns on large non-cash transfers, with penalties for noncompliance.

drawbacks.text: The bill replaces the step-up in basis at death with carryover basis, so heirs inherit the decedent's original cost basis; new information returns are required for non-cash assets over $1.3 million transferred at death, with penalties up to $10,000 per failure to report.

Under the bill's own schedule the tax would only apply above a $1 million exemption by 2006, meaning the repeal's benefits concentrate on the largest estates while the lost revenue is borne broadly by everyone else.

Critics in the House argued targeted relief for family farms and small businesses was already achievable without full repeal: the Democratic motion to recommit would have instead raised exemptions for small farms and businesses, and it failed 192-235 with 191 Democrats in favor and no Republicans.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief for family farms and closely held businesses is real but narrow: under the bill's own exemption schedule most of the money goes to estates at the very top of the wealth distribution. Replacing the step-up in basis with carryover basis adds genuine compliance burdens and can hit heirs of modest estates with capital gains they never realized themselves. The Rangel-Pomeroy alternative — higher exemptions for small farms and businesses rather than across-the-board repeal — addressed the stated family-business problem at a fraction of the revenue cost, and it was voted down.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 274-154, but Senate leaders never allowed an up-or-down vote — the bill sat on the Senate calendar, was laid before the Senate in June 2002, and was returned to the calendar without a vote; the estate-tax phase-out was instead enacted inside the broader 2001 tax cut law (H.R. 1836).

narrative.text: Introduced March 14, 2001 with 224 cosponsors, the bill cleared the Ways and Means Committee 24-14 on March 29 and was reported to the House on April 3.
On April 4, 2001 the House passed it 274-154: 215 of 219 voting Republicans in favor, 58 of 210 voting Democrats in favor.
A Democratic motion to recommit with instructions — substituting higher exemptions for small farms and businesses for full repeal — failed 192-235, with 191 Democrats in favor and zero Republicans.

The Senate received the bill on April 5 and placed it on the calendar, but never voted on it; in June 2002 the Senate laid it before itself and returned it to the calendar under a prior standing order.
The House action history cross-references H.R. 1836, the broad 2001 tax cut law, which is where the estate-tax phase-out was ultimately enacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Heirs to the country's largest estates. The standalone repeal never became law, but the same policy was enacted inside the 2001 tax cut law, phasing the estate tax down through 2010 — so large estates got the rate cuts and temporary repeal that the House had voted for here.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Heirs to the largest estates, via the 2001 tax law

for.name: Rep. Jennifer Dunn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through committee and floor passage.

for.name: 224 House cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors (32 of 208 House Democrats, 191 of 223 House Republicans, 1 Independent)

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Campaign for repeal and included the estate-tax phase-out in his 2001 tax cut, which he signed into law.

against.name: Rep. Charles Rangel
against.role: Ranking Member, House Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Offered a substitute amendment in the nature of a replacement, debated under the rule on the floor.

against.name: Rep. Earl Pomeroy
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit with instructions — the substitute keeping the tax with higher exemptions for small farms and businesses; it failed 192-235.

against.name: Sen. Tom Daschle
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled H.R. 8 for a Senate vote during the 107th Congress; the bill sat on the calendar and was returned to the calendar without action.

sides.party_line_note: Republicans backed the bill nearly unanimously (215-3), while Democrats split: 58 voted for final passage, but 191 of 210 voting Democrats supported the Democratic substitute that raised exemptions for small farms and businesses instead of full repeal — that substitute failed on party lines, 0 Republicans in favor.

industries.note: The bill zeroes out the tax that falls on large inheritances, with the bill's own exemption schedule showing the tax only applying above $1 million by 2006. The lost revenue is collected from a small set of the wealthiest families and has to be made up by everyone else.

industries.industry: Estate-planning attorneys and trust and wealth-advisory firms
industries.note: Full repeal removes much of the tax complexity that estate planning lives on, but the decade-long phase-in, new rate schedules, generation-skipping rules, and carryover-basis reporting requirements create substantial transition and compliance work.

industries.industry: Family farms and closely held family businesses
industries.note: These are the bill's stated beneficiaries: extended payment eligibility is widened to businesses with up to 45 partners or shareholders, and the conservation-easement estate tax rule is expanded. In practice, the rising exemption already shielded many such estates from owing any tax.
